summary:
Mpumalanga is geographically attributable as the institutional home of the National House of Traditional Leaders' (NHTL) formal campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. The NHTL—South Africa's official body of tribal chiefs—met at Hazyview, Mpumalanga, and resolved that "traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts," and separately asked Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Daily Maverick commentary identifies this NHTL lobbying, together with the chair of the Constitutional Review Committee, as precisely the mechanism that "intensifies prejudice and hatred" and fuels homophobic violence—an identified official-climate pathway, not merely a statement.

The dossier notes this evidence dates from 2010–2016 and should be treated as durable climate rather than current enacted policy. No provincial statute, no enforcement against a visitor, and no trans-specific incident series is documented. Mpumalanga is not listed in the former-Bantustan traditional-court geography; its risk signal is the formal institutional position taken on its soil, not a parallel legal system operating on visitors. South Africa's Constitution, PEPUDA, and the Hate Crime framework remain uniform and protective at the national level.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), Mpumalanga sits higher because KZN adds both a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA episode with an ongoing traditional-court jurisdiction question; Mpumalanga's finding is one resolution and its subsequent lobbying, geographically located but not jurisdictionally operationalised against visitors. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap is driven by the absence of a metro NGO belt and the NHTL's public rejection of the equality clause versus the Cape's institutional visibility. vs. Gauteng (0.71), Mpumalanga lacks the representative hate-crime research infrastructure that signals an active civil-society response environment.

sources.summary: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (missing from cache); the underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Daily Maverick commentary (25 May 2012, Mandy De Waal, interviewing constitutional-law professor Pierre de Vos): as the NHTL lobbies to remove gay rights from the Constitution and the chair of the Constitutional Review Committee makes anti-gay statements, lesbians and gays continue to be subject to violent attacks (citing the Noxolo Nogwaza 2011 and Eudy Simelane 2008 corrective-rape murders) - the traditional-leader lobbying identified as the fuel that fires homophobia.

tangentialFactors: The NHTL campaign targets the constitutional sexual-orientation equality clause and 'same-sex marriage' - an LGBT+-broad official-climate signal rather than a trans-specific measure; its documented spill-over is onto homophobic violence generally.
